report:
### Evidence Overview

Extensive, high-quality scientific research demonstrates that receiving an increasing number of childhood vaccines or vaccine antigens does **not** cause or increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

### Key Findings from Scientific Literature

* **Antigen Burden:** Concerns that "too many vaccines too soon" overwhelm the immune system have been directly tested. A landmark study evaluating cumulative exposure to vaccine antigens (proteins and polysaccharides) during infancy and early childhood found no association between total antigen exposure and the development of autism (https://www.jpeds.com/article/s0022-3476(13)00144-3/fulltext).
* **Childhood Immunization Schedule:** An independent review by the Institute of Medicine (IOM) examined the safety of the entire U.S. childhood vaccination schedule. The committee concluded that the recommended schedule is safe and found no evidence linking the cumulative schedule to autism or other neurodevelopmental disorders (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/01/130116123527.htm).
* **Systematic CDC & Global Studies:** Broad epidemiological research examining specific vaccines (such as MMR), components (such as thimerosal), and the overall number of immunizations consistently shows no causal connection between vaccination and autism (https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/vaccinesafety/00_pdf/CDCStudiesonVaccinesandAutism.pdf).

### Conclusion

Major health and scientific institutions—including the Institute of Medicine, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the American Academy of Pediatrics—unanimously conclude that the scientific evidence does not support the claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism.
